papers.title: Danger Detection Through Audio Captioning and Classification Fusion
papers.abstract: Sound is inherently ambiguous, which makes certainty critical in danger recognition, where false alarms and missed detection both carry real consequences. The definition of danger adopted here extends beyond ISO 7731:2003, which covers only intentionally designed alarm signals, to naturally occurring dangerous events such as glass breaking, gunshots, and human distress sounds, following the acoustic surveillance literature. Existing systems largely treat danger as multiclass classification without semantic reasoning about context, or rely on one-shot audio-to-word predictions that do not describe the scene. We instead treat danger as an outcome of the full acoustic scene, requiring semantically rich descriptions. The proposed framework trains a CNN for binary danger/no-danger classification on ESC-50, UrbanSound8K, and AudioSet, and in parallel extracts captions with the pretrained CoNeTTE model, scores them through a custom danger lexicon with SBERT similarity, and fine-tunes a DistilBERT classifier on the resulting labeled captions. The two classifiers are combined through a rule-based uncertainty fusion strategy, in which an inexpensive first-stage decision resolves clear-cut cases and the semantic classifier is reserved for ambiguous ones, reflecting the low-cost deployment demands of practical systems. On UrbanSound8K, fusion achieves a danger class recall of 0.88 (F1 0.66), improving over the standalone CNN (recall 0.70) and matching the semantic classifier alone (0.86) while invoking it for only 45% of clips, at about half of its measured computational cost, and preserving a human-readable intermediate description of each decision. We further evaluate the rule on two external, unseen datasets (XD-Violence and DESED) from different acoustic domains to assess generalization.

papers.title: A Generative Artificial Intelligence-Based Mechanism for Mobile Conversational Interaction in Japanese Language Learning
papers.abstract: Japanese language learning has long been constrained by acquisition difficulties arising from linguistic distance and by the limited availability of authentic opportunities for conversational interaction. Although mobile learning technologies offer considerable potential to alleviate these constraints, existing tools remain largely focused on vocabulary acquisition and grammar practice, while the dynamic progression of learner–artificial intelligence conversational interaction has received insufficient attention. In this study, a mobile Japanese conversational interaction system powered by a large language model was developed and integrated with automatic speech recognition and speech synthesis interfaces. Multi-topic conversational environments were constructed for learners at different proficiency levels. A four-week experiment involving 76 learners of Japanese was conducted, and interaction logs, JapaneseLanguage Proficiency Test–aligned mock assessments, and expert ratings were collected to characterize trajectories of conversation deepening and examine their associations with language learning outcomes. Pseudotime trajectory inference based on a minimum spanning tree demonstrated high internal consistency and external validity, and the composite conversation-depth score accounted for 43.8% of the variance in learner performance. Within individual conversational sessions, conversation depth increased significantly as the number of interactions turns increased. Intermediate learners exhibited greater mean pseudotime progression, more branch points, and faster rates of conversation deepening than beginner learners. These findings demonstrate that temporal modeling of interaction trajectories can be used to represent conversation deepening in generative artificial intelligence–supported mobile Japanese language learning as a quantifiable dynamic process. This approach provides a quantitative basis for investigating mobile conversation-based learning mechanisms and informing the design of adaptive conversational interactions.

papers.title: DO NATURAL AO ARTIFICIAL: A ASCENSÃO DA CLONAGEM DE VOZ E O FUTURO DA AUTENTICIDADE VOCAL
papers.abstract: This article aims to analyses voice cloning techniques through an exploratory study of the multilingual zero-shot XTTS-v2 model in the context of Brazilian Portuguese. Thirty synthetic samples were produced based on three reference conditions of approximately 8, 14, and 28 seconds, and subsequently compared with human recordings using acoustic-prosodic descriptors. The reference condition of 28 s showed the lowest mean distance and dispersion in the exploratory index, suggesting greater stability under this condition. While variation was observed across the generated samples and the index does not directly measure vocal naturalness or voice identity, the results still indicate that short reference samples can already produce synthetic speech that approximates acoustic and prosodic properties of the original voice. The findings reinforce the value of multidimensional analysis of vocal identity, contributing to discussing the limitations and impacts of voice cloning and to studies on synthetic speech detection in Brazilian Portuguese.

papers.title: Assesment of Multilingual Automatic Speech Recognition for Swahili, Kikuyu and Kalenjin Languages
papers.abstract: Language barriers continue to limit equitable access to digital and AI-assisted healthcare services, particularly for speakers of indigenous and low-resource languages. While Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) has achieved significant progress for high-resource languages, its performance remains insufficiently explored for many Kenyan local languages due to limited and inconsistent speech datasets. This study investigates the development and evaluation of a multilingual ASR system for three languages spoken in Kenya: Swahili, Kikuyu (Gĩkũyũ), and Kalenjin. The study focuses on assessing the capability of a unified ASR model to recognize speech across these linguistically diverse languages while addressing the challenges associated with low-resource language processing. Speech datasets are acquired, prepared, and standardized for model fine-tuning and evaluation. The performance of the developed ASR system is assessed using Word Error Rate (WER) and Character Error Rate (CER), enabling comparative analysis of recognition accuracy across the three languages. The study further considers practical deployment requirements, including computational efficiency and suitability for real-world multilingual applications. By providing a focused evaluation of ASR performance for Swahili, Kikuyu, and Kalenjin, this research contributes to the growing body of work on speech technologies for underrepresented African languages. The findings are expected to identify language-specific recognition challenges and establish a foundation for integrating reliable multilingual speech interfaces into AI-assisted healthcare and other accessibility-focused applications.

papers.title: Demystifying Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Health care: Is AI Friend or Foe?
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT The literature review is saturated with positive tones about the use of AI not only in health care but also in all aspects of our daily lives as well. The positivity range is extensive, ranging from increased accuracy, efficiency, productivity, profitability to creativity, equity, and advancement. Yet, the public is circumspect with continual exposure to news about cybersecurity threats or attacks, identity theft, violations of privacy, and challenges of establishing trust in their daily encounters with technology amidst prevalence of deep fakes, voice cloning, and AI-generated images or videos of people. A meta-synthesis of AI-related literature inclusive of expert panels is examined as an exploratory search for AI applicability and use in the health care landscape. The purpose of this article is to demystify AI highlighting areas of its use in health care, ways for clinicians specifically, care managers to bridge that divide and ascertain key practice standards with emphasis on its ethical use in health care. The settings using AI that were considered in this article include Health plans, Hospitals, medical practices or clinics, and Hospitals' Revenue Cycle Management (RCM). Implications and recommendations for case management engagement in AI are addressed relative to the standards of practice (SOPs).

## Model Description

**Luciole-8B-Audio-1.0** is an audio-capable version of [Luciole-8B-Instruct-1.1](https://huggingface.co/OpenLLM-France/Luciole-8B-Instruct-1.1).
The model was developed by [LINAGORA](https://linagora.com) and
the [OpenLLM-France](https://huggingface.co/OpenLLM-France) consortium, as part of the OpenLLM France project funded by
[BPI France](https://www.bpifrance.fr/) under the France 2030 program.

The training of Luciole-8B-Audio-1.0 was conducted on the Jean Zay supercomputer managed by [IDRIS](http://www.idris.fr/docs/idris/missions),
using the [NVIDIA NeMo Speech](https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Speech) toolkit.
The model was trained on various tasks and types of audio, including ASR (Automatic Speech Recognition), AST (Automatic Speech Translation), QA (Question Answering), Sound (Question Answering and Captioning), Music (Question Answering and Captioning) and more.

### Bias, Risks, and Limitations

- Inherits the limitations of the base [Luciole-8B-Instruct-1.1](https://huggingface.co/OpenLLM-France/Luciole-8B-Instruct-1.1)
  language model: it can struggle with math word problems and is susceptible to hallucination.
- Training sequences were capped at 16,384 tokens (audio and text combined), so longer contexts are untested.
<!-- - The audio encoder and its front-end were entirely frozen during training, so audio understanding is bounded by what
  Parakeet-TDT-0.6B-v3 already hears: the model cannot learn to compensate for acoustic conditions the
  encoder itself handles poorly. -->
- Language coverage is uneven. French and English make up most of the training mix and are the only languages seen on every task. German, Spanish and Italian were seen in training for ASR, AST and spoken QA. Portuguese, Dutch and Arabic for ASR and AST only.
- Arabic is the weakest language: the frozen Parakeet-TDT-0.6B-v3 encoder was not trained on Arabic,
  so the model is clearly less reliable there (FLEURS WER ~30%).
<!-- - LoRA fine-tuning only touches attention projections in the LLM; no additional audio-specific safety or
  refusal tuning was performed beyond what the base LLM already has. -->

### Recommendations

- Speech, sound and music understanding (summarization, captioning, sound/music QA, conversation):
  best in French and English, the only languages the model was trained on for these tasks.
- Transcription (ASR) and translation (AST): supported in French, English, German, Spanish,
  Italian, Portuguese and Dutch. For production ASR/AST pipelines, a dedicated model may still
  perform better.
- Spoken question answering: mainly supported in French and English. German, Spanish and
  Italian are also supported, but with far less training data.
- Other languages and tasks: outside French and English, evaluate the model on your own data
  before relying on it, especially for a task the model was not trained on in that language.
- Up-to-date or domain-specific knowledge: as with the base LLM, pair the model with a RAG
  pipeline.

## Training details

### Training data

Trained on the [OpenLLM-France/Luciole-Audio-Training-Dataset](https://huggingface.co/datasets/OpenLLM-France/Luciole-Audio-Training-Dataset),
a large multilingual, multi-task collection of audio–text conversations comprising: ASR (Automatic Speech Recognition),
AST (Automatic Speech Translation), spoken question answering, summarization, diarization, temporal localization,
speaker/gender/age/emotion/language recognition, and music/sound captioning and QA (Question Answering).

### Instruction template

Same chat template as the base LLM (inspired by Qwen3), extended with an `<|audio|>` locator tag:
wherever `<|audio|>` appears in a turn, the corresponding audio segment is encoded and its embeddings
replace the tag before the sequence reaches the LLM. Conversations can carry several audio clips and mix
audio-only, text-only, and audio+text turns within the same dialogue (see the
[dataset card](https://huggingface.co/datasets/OpenLLM-France/Luciole-Audio-Training-Dataset) for example
conversations).

### Training Procedure

| Component | Details |
|---|---|
| **Audio encoder** | [Parakeet-TDT-0.6B-v3](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/parakeet-tdt-0.6b-v3) Conformer encoder, frozen |
| **RoTE** | Applied between audio encoder and audio adapter. θ=1200, rotary fraction=0.2. Inspired by [Goel et al., 2024, OMCAT](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.12109).|
| **Audio adapter** | Linear projection into the LLM embedding space (1024 -> 4096) |
| **LLM** | [Luciole-8B-Instruct-1.1](https://huggingface.co/OpenLLM-France/Luciole-8B-Instruct-1.1), adapted with LoRA (on `q_proj`/`v_proj`, `up_proj`, `down_proj`, r=64, α=64) |
| **Trainable params** | 82.1M / ~8.2B (1.0%) |
| **Optimizer** | AdamW (β=(0.9, 0.98), weight decay 0.001) |
| **LR schedule** | Cosine annealing (max LR 2e-4, min LR 1e-6, 500 warmup steps) |
| **Batching** | Dynamic, bucketed by audio duration (27 buckets) |
| **Steps** | 100,000 |
| **Gradient clipping** | 1.0 |
| **Strategy** | FSDP2 (full sharding), activation checkpointing on the LLM (to allow for long sequences), 1 node × 4 H100 |
| **Precision** | bf16 |

The model was trained for 100k steps and drew from a weighted, randomly-ordered, sharded mix of that dataset,
bucketed by duration into 27 buckets (up to 1,200s / 16,384 audio-equivalent tokens per example) with a
matching dynamic batch size per bucket (238 down to 1).

Validation covered CommonVoice ASR (fr/en/ar),
Multilingual TEDx speech translation (fr→en), spoken QA (SLUE-SQA-5, VoxPopuli-QA, en/fr), and audio/music
captioning (AudioCaps, MusicCaps).

The training code and configs are available in the [Luciole-Audio-Training repository](https://github.com/OpenLLM-France/Luciole-Audio-Training). Training used an updated version of [NeMo/Speech 3.1](https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Speech) which can be found in our [NeMo/Speech fork](https://github.com/linagora-labs/NeMo/tree/luciole_speech.3.1.0-rc0).

## Evaluation

To evaluate our models and compare them with other open-weight Audio LLMs, we used [our fork of AudioBench](https://github.com/OpenLLM-France/AudioBench). We used a combination of datasets from AudioBench and datasets available in [our HF audio evaluation repository](https://huggingface.co/datasets/OpenLLM-France/Luciole-Audio-Evaluation-Dataset). You can find the full details and results on [our AudioBench leaderboard](https://openllm-france.github.io/AudioBench/).

A small excerpt from the leaderboard, showing the main table across all tasks and languages:

![results.png](assets/results.png)

Results for French and English only, as well as for ASR, AST, and QA tasks only:

![results_fr_en.png](assets/results_fr_en.png)

As you can see, the model [OpenLLM-France/Luciole-8B-Audio-1.0](https://huggingface.co/OpenLLM-France/Luciole-8B-Audio-1.0) performs well in French and English compared to other models.

For more detailed results in French ASR you can take a look at our [🏆 French ASR Leaderboard](https://linagora-labs.github.io/asr_benchmark/) where we use various types of datasets to evaluate the open source models. 


## Using the model

### With vLLM

The exported checkpoint's `config.json` declares `"model_type": "nemo_speechlm"` and
`"architectures": ["NeMoSpeechLMForConditionalGeneration"]`. Both are registered with vLLM by the SALM
plugin that ships inside `nemo-toolkit`
([`nemo.collections.speechlm2.vllm.salm`](https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Speech/tree/main/nemo/collections/speechlm2/vllm/salm))
via the `vllm.general_plugins` entry point:

```toml
[project.entry-points."vllm.general_plugins"]
nemo_speechlm = "nemo.collections.speechlm2.vllm.salm:register"
```

vLLM auto-discovers this plugin at startup as soon as `nemo-toolkit` and `vllm` are installed in the same
environment. The plugin merges the
LoRA adapters into the LLM backbone on load and runs the frozen Parakeet encoder + connector to turn each
`<|audio|>` tag into the right number of audio-embedding slots before generation.

**Install using uv**

```bash
uv venv .venv --python 3.12
source .venv/bin/activate

uv pip install "nemo-toolkit[speechlm2,tts] @ git+https://github.com/linagora-labs/NeMo.git@luciole-1b-vllm-nemotron-fix"
uv pip install vllm==0.28.0
uv pip install "numpy<=2.4"
```

**Serve**

```bash
vllm serve OpenLLM-France/Luciole-8B-Audio-1.0 \
    --max-model-len 16384
```

**Query** (OpenAI-compatible chat API, audio sent as base64):

```python
import base64
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="http://localhost:8000/v1", api_key="EMPTY")

with open("sample.wav", "rb") as f:   # 16 kHz mono
    audio_b64 = base64.b64encode(f.read()).decode()

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="OpenLLM-France/Luciole-8B-Audio-1.0",
    messages=[
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": [
                {"type": "text", "text": "Transcris cet audio en français : <|audio|>"},
                {"type": "input_audio", "input_audio": {"data": audio_b64, "format": "wav"}},
            ],
        }
    ],
)
print(response.choices[0].message.content)
```

The `<|audio|>` placeholder is the same `audio_locator_tag` used during training: put it in the text
wherever the audio should be attended to; the plugin expands it automatically. Audio must be 16 kHz mono;
the encoder supports chunked processing for long-form audio (well beyond the durations seen in training).

### With NeMo

The checkpoint can also be loaded directly with NeMo's `SALM` class
([`nemo.collections.speechlm2.models.salm`](https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Speech/blob/main/nemo/collections/speechlm2/models/salm.py)).

**Install**

```bash
uv venv .venv --python 3.12
source .venv/bin/activate

uv pip install "nemo-toolkit[speechlm2,tts] @ git+https://github.com/linagora-labs/NeMo.git@luciole-1b-vllm-nemotron-fix"
```

**Load and generate:**

```python
import torch
from nemo.collections.speechlm2 import SALM

model = SALM.from_pretrained("OpenLLM-France/Luciole-8B-Audio-1.0")  # or a local checkpoint directory
model = model.eval().to(torch.bfloat16).to("cuda")

# High-level API: pass the audio file path(s) directly in the prompt, next to the
# `<|audio|>` placeholder; SALM loads and resamples the audio for you.
answer_ids = model.generate(
    prompts=[
        [
            {
                "role": "user",
                "content": f"Transcris cet audio en français : {model.audio_locator_tag}",
                "audio": ["sample.wav"],
            }
        ]
    ],
    max_new_tokens=256,
)
print(model.tokenizer.ids_to_text(answer_ids[0].tolist()))
```

A prompt can carry several turns and several audio clips (one `<|audio|>` tag per clip, in order).

### Example prompts for each task

- ASR: 
  - English: `Make a word-for-word transcription in English of the spoken content.`
  - French: `Fais une transcription mot pour mot en français du contenu parlé.`
  - German: `Erstelle eine wortwörtliche Transkription des gesprochenen Inhalts auf Deutsch.`
  - Spanish: `Haz una transcripción palabra por palabra en español del contenido hablado.`
  - Italian: `Fai una trascrizione parola per parola in italiano del contenuto parlato.`
  - Portuguese: `Faça uma transcrição palavra por palavra em português do conteúdo falado.`
  - Dutch: `Maak een woord-voor-woord transcriptie in het Nederlands van de gesproken inhoud.`
  - No language given: `Can you write the text of this audio file in its source language?`
- QA: `Listen to the audio and answer the question.`
- AST: `Translate this file into French.`
- Diarization: 
  - `Provide a time-stamped, speaker-attributed transcript of this audio.`
  - `Transcris et diarise cet enregistrement, avec les horodatages de chaque tour.`

# Model Overview ### Description NVIDIA Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe is an offline speech and audio model that processes recordings, together with text instructions and optional context, into text responses. NVIDIA developed this [Speech-Augmented Language Model (SALM)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.09424) for multilingual transcription, speech translation, contextual transcription, speaker-attributed transcription, rich transcription, timestamp prediction, language identification, and audio question answering. The training mixture also includes a small amount of text instruction following and PII tagging/redaction tasks. This model is ready for commercial or non-commercial use. ### Model Summary | | | |:---|:---| | **Total Parameters** | 34B (4.3B active), including the audio encoder | | **Architecture** | Mamba-2–Transformer hybrid Mixture of Experts language model with a Parallel Expert Encoder (Transformer ASR encoder and speaker encoder) | | **Precision** | BF16 (full-precision reference weights); [FP8](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B-FP8) and [NVFP4](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B-NVFP4) variants are available | | **Context Length** | 65,536 tokens; recordings up to 1 hour | | **Inputs / Outputs** | Audio and text / text, with optional word timestamps | | **Languages** | 40; see the [language support matrix](#language-support-matrix) | | **Tasks** | Transcription in verbatim or written form, contextual transcription, speaker-attributed transcription, rich transcription, speech translation, language identification, and audio question answering | | **Deployment** | 1× H100 80 GB; see the [hardware compatibility table](#software-integration) | | **Speculative Decoding** | Native Multi-Token Prediction (MTP); optional DFlash2 draft model | | **Reasoning Mode** | Configurable through the chat template (`enable_thinking=True/False`) | | **Recommended Sampling** | Transcription, translation, and language identification: temperature 0, reasoning off; audio understanding: temperature 0.6, top_p 0.95, reasoning on | | **Best For** | Highest accuracy, customization, and fine-tuning | | **License** | [OpenMDW-1.1](https://openmdw.ai/license/1-1/) | ### Results at a Glance Results captured on October 12, 2026. Install both into one environment with [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) and download the checkpoint: ```bash git clone https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Speech.git nemo-speech cd nemo-speech uv venv --python 3.13 .venv UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=$PWD/.venv uv sync --extra asr --extra vllm --locked --no-install-project uv pip install --python .venv/bin/python --no-deps -e . # PyAV decodes compressed audio formats, such as M4A, without a system FFmpeg. uv pip install --python .venv/bin/python --no-deps av==19.0.2 # vLLM requires OpenCV, which NeMo's dependency settings exclude. uv pip install --python .venv/bin/python --no-deps opencv-python-headless==5.0.0.93 source .venv/bin/activate hf download nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B --local-dir ./NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B ``` #### Start the Server Start an OpenAI-compatible server on one GPU, with MTP speculative decoding proposing eight tokens (MTP8): ```bash export VLLM_PLUGINS=nemo_speechlm # Allow vLLM to decode recordings up to one hour long (the default is 600 seconds). export VLLM_MAX_AUDIO_DECODE_DURATION_S=3600 export VLLM_MAX_AUDIO_CLIP_FILESIZE_MB=180 # Word timestamps require the V1 model runner. export VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=0 vllm serve ./NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B \ --served-model-name nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B \ --trust-remote-code --dtype bfloat16 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.94 \ --max-model-len 65536 --max-num-batched-tokens 4096 --max-num-seqs 192 \ --enable-chunked-prefill --no-enable-prefix-caching \ --use-replayssm --mamba-backend flashinfer --mamba-cache-mode none \ --mm-processor-cache-gb 0 --no-async-scheduling \ --limit-mm-per-prompt '{"audio":{"count":6,"length":120000000}}' \ --speculative-config '{"method":"mtp","num_speculative_tokens":8}' \ --reasoning-parser nemotron_v3 \ --trust-request-mm-kwargs \ --middleware nemo.collections.speechlm2.vllm.salm.ctc_serving.ctc_timestamp_middleware ``` The server listens on `127.0.0.1:8000`; use `--host` and `--port` to change this. The settings target an H100 with 80 GB of GPU memory; other hardware or workloads may need a different `--gpu-memory-utilization`, `--max-model-len`, or `--max-num-seqs`. The `--middleware` and `--trust-request-mm-kwargs` options let requests opt into [word timestamps](#word-timestamps-and-speaker-diarization). To change the configuration, modify the command as follows: | Configuration | Change | | --- | --- | | Eight GPUs: one data-parallel engine per GPU, with expert parallelism (TP=1, DP=8, EP=8) | Add `--data-parallel-size 8 --api-server-count 8 --enable-expert-parallel --disable-custom-all-reduce` | | MTP with two proposed tokens (MTP2) | Set `"num_speculative_tokens":2` | | No speculative decoding | Remove `--speculative-config` | #### Speculative Decoding Speculative decoding proposes several tokens at once and verifies them with the main model. The checkpoint contains two MTP depths implemented with a repeated layer. MTP8 reuses that layer to propose eight tokens; it does not require eight distinct trained MTP layers. The best mode depends on the GPU and the workload. Approximate throughput for batched English ASR on **one NVIDIA H100 80 GB**, using tuned serving settings: | Decoding mode | Approximate BF16 RTFx | | --- | ---: | | MTP off | Not measured | | MTP2 | 410 | | MTP8 | 270 | | DFlash2 K=7 | 340 | | DFlash2 K=15 | 260 | RTFx is total audio duration divided by processing time: 340 RTFx means about 340 seconds of audio processed per second under batch load. These are rough throughput estimates, excluding server startup, for the English Open ASR and Monsoon datasets with reasoning disabled. Throughput depends on recording length, output length, batch size, and GPU memory settings; it is not a single-request latency estimate. Keep ReplaySSM (`--use-replayssm --mamba-backend flashinfer --mamba-cache-mode none`) and prefix caching disabled, as in the command above. The first requests after startup are slower while kernels are compiled and warmed up.
DFlash2 draft model As an alternative to MTP, the separate draft model [`nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B-DFlash2`](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B-DFlash2) proposes up to 15 tokens at once with vLLM's `dflash` method. DFlash2 and MTP are alternatives and are not combined. K=7 is the recommended starting point; K=15 was slower on the tested ASR workload. vLLM 0.32.0 needs a small fix to its DFlash2 implementation; without it, the server can fail when requests finish. Apply it once to the environment: ```bash python - <<'EOF_PATCH' from pathlib import Path import vllm path = Path(vllm.__file__).parent / "model_executor/models/qwen3_dflash2.py" source = path.read_text() if "safe_anchor_token_ids" not in source: old = " successors = successor_table[candidate_ids]\n" anchor = " anchor_token_ids[:, None, None].expand(-1, 1, top_k)," assert source.count(old) == 1 and source.count(anchor) == 1, "unexpected vLLM version" source = source.replace(old, ( " safe_anchor_token_ids = anchor_token_ids.clamp(\n" " min=0, max=predecessor_table.shape[0] - 1\n" " )\n" + old )).replace(anchor, " safe_anchor_token_ids[:, None, None].expand(-1, 1, top_k),") path.write_text(source) EOF_PATCH ``` The fix modifies vLLM source code (Copyright contributors to the vLLM project), which is licensed under the Apache License, Version 2.0, not under OpenMDW-1.1; see [THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md](THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md). Then start the server with the following options instead of `--speculative-config` and `--middleware` from the command above. Word timestamps are not available with DFlash2, so the CTC alignment is disabled: ```bash --speculative-config '{"method":"dflash","num_speculative_tokens":7,"model":"nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B-DFlash2"}' \ --hf-overrides '{"ctc_timestamps":{"enabled":false}}' ``` vLLM runs DFlash2 only on its V2 model runner, so also run `unset VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER` before starting the server.
#### Send a Request Send audio to the `/v1/chat/completions` endpoint with an OpenAI-compatible client. The following function covers transcription, reasoning, and word timestamps: ```python import base64 from pathlib import Path from openai import OpenAI client = OpenAI(base_url="http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1", api_key="EMPTY") def ask(audio_path, prompt, system_prompt="", reasoning=False, timestamps=False): audio = base64.b64encode(Path(audio_path).read_bytes()).decode() messages = [{"role": "system", "content": system_prompt}] if system_prompt else [] messages.append({"role": "user", "content": [ {"type": "text", "text": prompt}, {"type": "audio_url", "audio_url": {"url": f"data:audio/wav;base64,{audio}"}}, ]}) extra_body = { "chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": reasoning}, "skip_special_tokens": False, # keep speaker and event tags "spaces_between_special_tokens": False, "seed": 0, } if reasoning: extra_body.update(top_k=-1, thinking_token_budget=17408) extra_body["chat_template_kwargs"]["reasoning_budget"] = 16384 if timestamps: extra_body["mm_processor_kwargs"] = {"capture_ctc_timestamps": True} return client.chat.completions.create( model="nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B", messages=messages, temperature=0.6 if reasoning else 0, top_p=0.95 if reasoning else 1.0, max_tokens=20480 if reasoning else 16384, extra_body=extra_body, ) response = ask("audio.wav", "Transcribe the following audio.") print(response.choices[0].message.content) ``` A dense one-hour conversation can need about 20,000 output tokens. For long recordings, raise `max_tokens` or remove it, so that the transcript is not truncated. Transcription uses temperature 0 with reasoning disabled. For audio understanding, enable reasoning and ask a question about the audio: ```python response = ask("audio.wav", "What is happening in this audio?", reasoning=True) ``` This sets temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, top-k disabled, seed 0, a 20,480-token completion limit, and a 16,384-token reasoning budget with a 1,024-token allowance to finish reasoning. Use the task instructions documented under [Evaluation Prompts](#evaluation-prompts) as `prompt` and `system_prompt`. #### Word Timestamps and Speaker Diarization The checkpoint bundles the CTC heads used to align the generated transcript to the audio. With `--middleware` set as in the server command above, request timestamps with `timestamps=True`, together with a speaker-tagged transcription prompt: ```python response = ask("audio.wav", ( "Transcribe this audio with punctuation and capitalization. " "Include all spoken words and verbal fillers. " "Write numbers in their standard written form. " "Put speaker tags on the transcription." ), timestamps=True) alignment = response.model_dump()["ctc_timestamps"] if alignment["error"] is not None: raise RuntimeError(alignment["error"]) for word in alignment["words"]: print(word["word"], word["start"], word["end"], word["speaker"]) ``` The response contains a top-level `ctc_timestamps` object: - `words`: word text, start and end times in seconds relative to the input audio, and the transcript's speaker tag. - `diarization`: speaker activity segments derived from the audio. - `speaker_tag_to_diarization_speaker`: the mapping between transcript tags and diarization speakers. - `error`: `null` on success, or an alignment failure reason. Check this field before using the timestamps. Timestamp requests accept one audio recording, `stream=false`, and `n=1`. Keep `skip_special_tokens=false` and ask for speaker tags when speaker attribution is needed. A transcript without speaker tags is aligned as a single speaker. Use the `diarization` segments, rather than word timestamps, when evaluating diarization. ### SGLang-Omni [SGLang-Omni](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang-omni) serves this model for whole-file transcription on `/v1/audio/transcriptions`, on one GPU, from the BF16 or FP8 checkpoint (both validated on one H100 80 GB and one RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell). It does not need NeMo. After [installing SGLang-Omni](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang-omni/blob/main/docs/get_started/installation.md) 0.2.0, which pins SGLang 0.5.22: ```bash sgl-omni serve \ --model-path nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B \ --model-name nemotron-transcribe \ --mem-fraction-static 0.85 \ --port 8000 curl http://localhost:8000/v1/audio/transcriptions \ -F model=nemotron-transcribe \ -F file=@audio.wav ``` Word timestamps, speaker-attributed output, translation and speculative decoding are not part of this integration. See the [SGLang-Omni Nemotron Transcribe cookbook](https://sgl-project.github.io/sglang-omni/cookbook/nemotron_transcribe.html) for its settings, streaming and a tuned profile for short clips. ### Transformers usage 🤗 Install 🤗 Transformers from source: ```sh pip install git+https://github.com/huggingface/transformers ```
Transcription ```python from transformers import AutoModelForMultimodalLM, AutoProcessor model_id = "nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B" samples = "https://huggingface.co/datasets/hf-internal-testing/dummy-audio-samples/resolve/main/" processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id) model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained(model_id, device_map="auto") audio = [samples + "en-Alice_woman.wav", samples + "diarization_example.mp3"] speaker_attributed_prompt = ( "Transcribe this audio with punctuation and capitalization. Include all spoken words and verbal fillers. Write " "numbers in their standard written form. Put speaker tags on the transcription." ) prompt = [None, speaker_attributed_prompt] inputs = processor.apply_transcription_request(audio, prompt=prompt).to(model.device) outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=1024) texts = processor.decode(outputs[:, inputs.input_ids.shape[1] :], skip_special_tokens=False) print([text.replace(processor.tokenizer.pad_token, "") for text in texts]) ```
Speaker-attributed transcription ```python from transformers import AutoModelForMultimodalLM, AutoProcessor model_id = "nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B" samples = "https://huggingface.co/datasets/hf-internal-testing/dummy-audio-samples/resolve/main/" processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id) model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained(model_id, device_map="auto") prompt = ( "Transcribe this audio with punctuation and capitalization. Include all spoken words and verbal fillers. Write " "numbers in their standard written form. Put speaker tags on the transcription." ) conversation = [ { "role": "user", "content": [ {"type": "text", "text": prompt}, {"type": "audio", "path": samples + "diarization_example.mp3"}, ], } ] inputs = processor.apply_chat_template( conversation, tokenize=True, add_generation_prompt=True, return_dict=True, enable_thinking=False, ).to(model.device) outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=1024) text = processor.decode(outputs[0, inputs.input_ids.shape[1] :], skip_special_tokens=False) print(text) ``` `processor.extract_speaker_dict` splits the output into one dictionary per speaker turn: ```python for turn in processor.extract_speaker_dict(text): print(turn) ```
Word timestamps and speaker diarization Requires `torchaudio` and `scipy`. ```python from transformers import AutoModelForMultimodalLM, AutoProcessor model_id = "nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B" samples = "https://huggingface.co/datasets/hf-internal-testing/dummy-audio-samples/resolve/main/" processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id) model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained(model_id, device_map="auto") prompt = ( "Transcribe this audio with punctuation and capitalization. Include all spoken words and verbal fillers. Write " "numbers in their standard written form. Put speaker tags on the transcription." ) inputs = processor.apply_transcription_request(samples + "diarization_example.mp3", prompt=prompt).to(model.device) outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=1024, return_word_timestamp_logits=True) texts = processor.decode(outputs.sequences[:, inputs.input_ids.shape[1] :], skip_special_tokens=False) timestamps = processor.align_word_timestamps( texts, outputs.word_timestamp_logits, inputs.input_features_mask, outputs.speaker_logits, ) print(timestamps[0]["chunks"][:3]) ```
See the [Transformers documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/nemotron3_5_transcribe) for more. ### Evaluation Prompts Use these shortened task-specific templates as starting points. For ASR evaluation, use [Exact ASR Benchmark Prompts](#exact-asr-benchmark-prompts). The ASR benchmark environment uses vLLM 0.28.0 and NeMo Speech with the FP32 preservation change from [PR #16357](https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Speech/pull/16357), which is included in the main branch, with MTP2. For audio understanding, spoken instructions, and text reasoning, use [Exact Understanding and Reasoning Prompts](#exact-understanding-and-reasoning-prompts), which lists the complete evaluated system prompts; keep the prepared user questions and choices unchanged. For the remaining benchmark families, use [All Evaluated Prompts](#all-evaluated-prompts), which contains the complete evaluated prompts and reasoning flags. Replace placeholders with the actual languages, labels, or context. #### Prompt Recommendations For these tasks, keep the **system prompt empty**. Send the instruction in the **user message**, alongside the audio. | Task | Recommended user prompt | Why we suggest it | | --- | --- | --- | | Verbatim ASR, including multilingual and long-form audio | `Audio transcription. Language: as spoken. Wording: verbatim, including fillers and repetitions. Formatting: punctuation and capitalization. Output: transcript only.` | Preserves wording and language with an explicit output format. | | Clean written transcript | Replace the wording clause above with `omit fillers and accidental repetitions; keep the remaining spoken wording unchanged`. Add `numbers in their standard written form` if needed. | Makes cleanup and number normalization explicit. | | Speaker attribution / word timestamps | `Transcribe this audio with punctuation and capitalization. Include all spoken words and verbal fillers. Write numbers in their standard written form. Put speaker tags on the transcription.` | Provides stable speaker tags for attribution and timestamp alignment; also enable timestamp capture. | | Near-field speaker only (experimental) | `Transcribe this audio. Include all spoken words and verbal fillers. Write numbers as spoken. No punctuation or capitalization. Transcribe only the speaker nearest to the microphone. Do not transcribe any other voices.` | Ignores background voices, such as far-field speech in a meeting room. With LibriSpeech test-clean speech mixed with far-field NOTSOFAR-1 audio, the WER is 4.78% with this prompt and 27.32% with a single-speaker transcription prompt. | | Code-switching / script control | `Transcribe verbatim in the original languages. Preserve hesitations and false starts. Write in

--- base_model: hexgrad/Kokoro-82M base_model_relation: adapter pipeline_tag: text-to-speech license: apache-2.0 language: - en datasets: - parler-tts/libritts_r_filtered - facebook/voxpopuli - amphion/Emilia-Dataset tags: - kokoro - voice-cloning - adapter - styletts2 - text-to-speech --- # kokoro-inno-clone-tuner ![banner](https://cdn-uploads.huggingface.co/production/uploads/6444c7a59174daa2f6934a16/_u14iRNVPEU0GA3z7jk48.png) ```python pip install inno-kokoro ``` Zero-shot voice tuner for [Kokoro-82M](https://huggingface.co/hexgrad/Kokoro-82M). Outputs base Kokoro compatible voice packs @ `[510, 1, 256]`. ([write-up](https://remsky.art/writeups/kokoro-fastapi/inno-clone/)) ## Samples Same passage for every voice, enrolled from the references. LibriTTS-R speakers are `dev-clean` held out from training. | voice | tuned | reference | |---|---|---| | am_libritts1272 | | | | af_libritts5338 | | | | am_libritts6241 | | | | af_ameliaearhart | | | | bf_janegoodall | | | | am_vincentprice | | | ## Usage Code available on Github: [remsky/inno-kokoro](https://github.com/remsky/inno-kokoro). Integrated into [Kokoro-FastAPI](https://github.com/remsky/Kokoro-FastAPI) (v0.9.0+) ```bash pip install inno-kokoro ``` Enrolling a voice: ```python from inno_kokoro.enroll import Tuner, enroll, read from kokoro import KPipeline tuner = Tuner() # pulls model.safetensors into the huggingface cache pack, _ = enroll(*read("my_ref.wav"), tuner) pipe = KPipeline(lang_code="a") wav = next(pipe("Hello from a tuned voice.", voice=pack)).audio ``` The pack is a plain tensor; `torch.save(pack, "voices/am_me.pt")` makes it a voice file like any other, prefixed by accent and gender like the stock packs. The pitch-tracking ceiling is set automatically from the reference's harmonic spacing, so band-limited or archival sources land in the right octave without tuning. - `enroll(..., fmax=180)` overrides it if a voice still reads the wrong register. ### Architecture A 5 to 30 s reference clip in, a stock-shaped Kokoro voice pack out. Everything loads from `model.safetensors`, no extra downloads.
Architecture details Enrollment embeds an input audio sample via the baked speaker encoder and maps through `model.safetensors` to build the encoder side; prosody aspects are measured to build the predictor half. - **speaker encoder**: a 6.6M-param WeSpeaker ResNet34 distilled from [**UniSpeech-SAT-sv**](https://huggingface.co/microsoft/unispeech-sat-base-plus-sv) embeddings - matches within 0.002 speaker cosine on hold-out dev-clean (380mb fp32 -> 14mb fp16) - **style head**: the decoder (timbre) half of the pack comes from the speaker embedding (512) mapped to Kokoro style (256). Shifts along a learned spectral-tilt direction by the reference's measured tilt. - **prosody blend**: the predictor (prosody) half uses the stock Kokoro packs as a foundation: - Blended by nonnegative least squares to the reference F0 mean, F0 spread and syllable rate. - Packs more than 4 st from the reference's pitch are excluded. - Higher graded packs are weighted as preferred during selection. - **prosody head** (v0.2): a linear adjust on the blend from the reference's F0 mean and spread, - fitted to deltas optimized through the frozen predictor. `enroll(..., head=False)` skips it. Enrollment runs in about 0.05 s per second of reference on CPU (a 30 s reference in 1.4 s) and 0.1-0.3 s total on a GPU, after the one-time model load. Total model size @ fp16: ~24mb
## Limits - English trained (LibriTTS-R) currently - Some texture/identity is traded to maintain audio quality and stability within Kokoro's range. - Rythym is a best-effort match to the speaker. - Prosody is a convex blend of stock prosody by pitch, spread and pace. Outside of that range, it will only pin to the nearest edge - Reference clip requirements: - 3 second minimum, up to a max of 30s - Reasonably free of audio artifacts - Single speaker ## Training and Metrics All stages: Kokoro frozen; LibriTTS-R train-clean-100 unless noted. Trained via HF Jobs `a10g-small`; under $20 in GPU time:
v0.1.0 training notes - Stage 1: mapped speaker embedding to timbre: - Style head on a speaker-embedding cycle loss: clone, render, re-embed, cosine to the input audio embedding. - [10k steps: dev cosine ~0.92; nearest stock voice baseline 0.857] - Stage 2: the embedding alone missed texture and pitch; adjustments: - Augmented pitch and speed. Added losses via a WavLM layer-statistics L1, a small log-F0 error, and spectral-tilt. - [11k steps: dev cosine 0.934, DNSMOS 3.30] - Stage 3: tuned the encoder side to match the blended predictors: - Predictor half fixed to the blended rows, only the decoder half trained. - [3k steps: dev cosine 0.932, DNSMOS 3.48] - Stage 4: distilled the speaker encoder so enrollment needs no UniSpeech download: - WeSpeaker ResNet34 plus a projection, trained on `1 - cos(student, teacher)` over LibriTTS-R crops with synthetic channel damage; the style head is untouched. - [20k steps: hold-out dev-clean parity, DNSMOS equal; archival references sat about 0.05 behind the teacher] - Stage 5: the student lagged the teacher on archival references; synthetic damage had plateaued: - Mixed real public-domain archival broadcast audio into the distillation crops. - [8k steps: archival cosine up 0.03-0.05, DNSMOS unchanged]
v0.2.0 training notes - Stage 1: the blend under-predicted pitch range and sentence-final falls: - Fitted a predictor-half delta per speaker (426; adds VoxPopuli-en and Emilia-YODAS EN) - Targeted F0 mean, spread, IQR, pause fraction and speech time. - Ridge head from reference F0 mean + spread to the fitted delta. - [hold-out: F0 mean error 0.9 -> 0.45 st, spread 0.6 -> 0.35 st, IQR 0.9 -> 0.5 st] - Stage 2: the student trailed the teacher on public-speaking and in-the-wild references: - Added VoxPopuli and Emilia speakers to the distillation crops. - [8k steps: hold-out cosine VoxPopuli 0.976 -> 0.986, Emilia 0.964 -> 0.983; WavLM cosine 0.941 -> 0.944, DNSMOS unchanged] - Stage 3: the timbre half had only seen LibriTTS speakers: - Repeated v0.1.0 stage 3 with VoxPopuli and Emilia speakers in the draw. - [3k steps: WavLM cosine samples 0.927 -> 0.935, dev-clean 0.956 -> 0.959, VoxPopuli 0.926 -> 0.939, Emilia 0.931 -> 0.936; DNSMOS unchanged]
### Zero-shot identity benchmark Inno gets about a third of the normalized similarity range, twice as close as the nearest stock pack (with UTMOS intact and keeping Kokoro's stable natural style).
Full benchmark results and methodology LibriSpeech test-clean, F5-TTS cross-sentence split (1127 utterances, 39 held-out speakers. Reference in, new sentence out, scored against the speaker's real recording. - normalized: how far the render sits between sounding like a stranger (0) and a second real take of the speaker (1) - RTF: RTX 4060 Ti | system | SIM-o | normalized | ECAPA | UTMOS | RTF | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | ground truth (second recording) | 0.695 | 1.00 | 0.656 | 4.10 | | | F5-TTS v1 base | 0.650 | 0.94 | 0.713 | 3.86 | 0.48 | | StyleTTS2 (LibriTTS zero-shot) | 0.386 | 0.46 | 0.415 | 4.40 | 0.06 | | **Inno v0.2** | 0.288 | 0.32 | 0.288 | 4.45 | 0.07 | | OpenVoice v2 | 0.227 | 0.23 | 0.316 | 3.80 | 0.12 | | Kokoro, nearest stock pack | 0.167 | 0.15 | 0.215 | 4.25 | 0.06 | StyleTTS2 uses a related architecture with an unfrozen decoder, a possible ceiling for this style space. - StyleTTS2: alpha 0.3, beta 0.7, 5 steps. - OpenVoice v2: MeloTTS EN-US, tau 0.3. - F5-TTS: 32 NFE, CFG 2.
v0.1 vs v0.2 shipped-weight comparison Measured on the shipped weights through the stock `KPipeline`: one fixed passage rendered for the seven sample voices plus ten hold-out dev-clean speakers, F0 by Praat over 6 s chunks with the reference's tracking ceiling applied to both sides. | metric | v0.1 blend only | v0.2 with head | |---|---|---| | speaker cosine (WavLM-sv), samples / dev-clean | 0.926 / 0.956 | 0.935 / 0.959 | | F0 mean, render minus reference | 0.65 st mean abs | 0.8 st mean abs | | F0 spread, render minus reference | 0.65 st mean abs | 0.5 st mean abs | | DNSMOS | 3.50 | 3.50 | The head's gain is spread; on F0 mean it scatters more per speaker and flips the signed bias from -0.2 to +0.3 st.
## Licenses and credits Adapter weights and code: Apache-2.0, except the baked speaker encoder (`enc.*` in `model.safetensors`), which is CC BY-SA 3.0 (see below) - Built on [hexgrad/Kokoro-82M](https://huggingface.co/hexgrad/Kokoro-82M) (Apache-2.0, StyleTTS2 architecture) - The speaker encoder is a [WeSpeaker](https://github.com/wenet-e2e/wespeaker) ResNet34 (code Apache-2.0) - initialised from the [VoxCeleb-trained ResNet34-LM weights](https://huggingface.co/Wespeaker/wespeaker-voxceleb-resnet34-LM) (CC BY 4.0) - distilled from [microsoft/unispeech-sat-base-plus-sv](https://huggingface.co/microsoft/unispeech-sat-base-plus-sv) - (Microsoft UniSpeech, [CC BY-SA 3.0 on GitHub](https://github.com/microsoft/UniSpeech/blob/main/LICENSE)); encoder weights under CC BY-SA 3.0 - Training data (no audio redistributed beyond the samples): - [LibriTTS-R](https://www.openslr.org/141/) (CC BY 4.0), also the LibriTTS sample references - [VoxPopuli](https://github.com/facebookresearch/voxpopuli) (CC0) - [Emilia-YODAS](https://huggingface.co/datasets/amphion/Emilia-Dataset) EN (CC BY 4.0) - Sample references: - Amelia Earhart from ["Speech by Amelia Earhart"](https://www.loc.gov/item/afccal000004/), Library of Congress AFC 1986/022 - Jane Goodall from [BBC Woman's Hour excerpt](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Jane_Goodall_BBC_Radio4_Woman%27s_Hour_26_Jan_2010_p00tr6ks.flac), BBC, CC BY 3.0 - Vincent Price public domain from ["The House On Haunted Hill"](https://archive.org/details/The_House_On_Haunted_Hill) Only clone voices you have permission to clone, even the shallow cloning offered via this model and technique.

# kurisu-v2proplus · AnifLive-TTS 便携模型包

这是 **AnifLive-TTS** 使用的 `kurisu-v2proplus` 模型包（GSV-v2ProPlus 架构，FP16），
已经去掉与本机显卡绑定的 TensorRT 引擎，只保留可跨机器复用的部分。

## 内容

```text
kurisu-v2proplus\      onnx\ + voices\ + manifest/source/checksums   ≈ 2.0 GiB
shared\                AnifLive 公共权重（BERT/SSL 等）                ≈ 1.0 GiB
```

- **不含** `engines\`：TensorRT 引擎的指纹包含 GPU 型号、显存、SM 数、CUDA/TensorRT 版本、平台，
  换机器无法复用，必须在本机重建。
- `manifest.json` 已移除 `active_engine_fingerprint`；`checksums.json` 按精简后的文件重新生成并通过校验。
- 本仓库**只提供模型文件**，不含 AnifLive-TTS 代码。

## 使用

```powershell
# 1. 下载到 AstrBot 仓库的 models\tts 下
hf download kuris1213/kurisu-v2proplus --local-dir models\tts

# 2. 在本机重建 TensorRT 引擎（需要 NVIDIA GPU + CUDA + TensorRT 11，10~30 分钟）
aniflive-tts model rebuild-engines --model-package models\tts\kurisu-v2proplus

# 3. 启动本地语音服务
aniflive-tts serve --host 127.0.0.1 --port 9882 `
  --model-package models\tts\kurisu-v2proplus `
  --shared-dir models\tts\shared
```

没有 NVIDIA 显卡无法使用：AnifLive-TTS 只有 TensorRT-11 后端，没有 CPU 推理路径。

- 模型音色基于角色「牧濑红莉栖」，角色与作品版权归原权利方；本仓库与权利方无关联。
- 仅供个人学习、研究与自托管；请勿商用、售卖或用于冒充他人。
- 使用本模型产生的任何后果由使用者自行承担。
